articles.text: The City of Piedmont announced on November 9 that it is seeking volunteers to serve on the Measure UU Bond Oversight Committee, established by City Council at its October 4 meeting. The committee will consist of five residents who will focus on reviewing and reporting on the expenditure of the proceeds of the bonds. The bonds for the project will be sold on November 18, and interest on the bonds is tax exempt with maturities ranging from 2023 through 2051. The committee will inform the public on how the city is expending the bond proceeds and review expenditure reports produced by the city. Committee members will produce an annual report which will include a statement indicating whether the bonds used are appropriate as set forth in Measure UU, and a summary of the committee’s proceedings and activities for the preceding year. The Bond Oversight Committee is not responsible for managing or directing any pool activities; instead, it will use the experience of its members to ensure bond proceeds are spent in accordance with Ordinance 754 N.S., or Measure UU, passed by voters in November 2020. The committee will meet two times per year throughout the project until the expenditure of the bond proceeds is complete, which is anticipated to be a 24 to 36-month process. Interested residents may download the Application for Appointive Vacancy or apply online on the City’s web site at https://piedmont.ca.gov. Applications are due to City Hall on or before Wednesday, December 8 at 5:00 p.m. Interviews with the City Council for the positions will be scheduled for the evening of Monday, December 13, 2021. No appointments will be made without a Council interview. Residents with questions are invited to contact the City Clerk’s office at (510) 420-3040.

articles.text: The Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD) is recommending booster shots of the COVID-19 vaccine for all people age 65 and older who received any of the three available vaccines. It also has recommended booster shots for older adults and certain groups who received Moderna, and all adults who received the Johnson and Johnson vaccine more than two months ago. “As family and friends make plans to gather in the coming months, we encourage everyone to get vaccinated as soon as possible,” ACPHD Public Information Officer Neetu Balram said. “Older adults and younger people with underlying conditions or certain other risk factors who received either Pfizer or Moderna more than six months ago can now get vaccine booster doses, and anyone who received Johnson & Johnson at least two months ago can also receive a booster.” Balram cites emerging evidence that suggests immunity from COVID-19 vaccination may wane over time. In October the Federal Drug Administration (FDA) authorized booster doses for people vaccinated with any of the three authorized COVID-19 vaccines and is highly recommending boosters for those over age 18 who received a Johnson and Johnson vaccine. Mixing and matching of booster is permitted by health officials, so recipients may choose a different vaccine for a booster than their original series. “COVID-19 vaccines have proven to be highly safe and effective, and booster doses will help ensure we get the greatest possible benefit,” said Dr. Nicholas Moss, Alameda County Public Health Director. “I strongly recommend getting a booster if you are 65 or older, live in a long-term care setting, or have an underlying medical condition which places you at higher risk for infection and severe illness.” As of November 8, 16% of eligible residents in Alameda County are unvaccinated, or haven’t received their second dose of a two-dose series. Where to go Any eligible person seeking a booster shot can consult with their medical provider, or go to a chain pharmacy like CVS, Walgreens, Rite Aid, Safeway, or Costco. A full list of vaccine-providing pharmacies in the area can be found at www. vaccines.gov. Some participating locations allow for walk-in appointments. Those who have not received any form of vaccination may create an appointment by visiting https://covid-19.acgov.org/vaccines.

articles.text: For over 30 years Piedmont Scouts have conducted a door-to-door Scouting for Food Drive prior to Thanksgiving, collecting non-perishable food for the Alameda County Community Food Bank. Door hangers were put at houses last weekend reminding residents that the food drive will be this Saturday, November 13, starting at 9 a.m. Residents are encouraged to leave donations of nutritious, non-perishable food in boxes or bags outside their front door. Food will be collected by Piedmont Scouts and delivered to a collection point staffed by Piedmont Scouting’s coed Venturing programs, including the Piedmont Community Service Crew, and the Alameda County Community Food Bank. In previous years, the Scouts collected more than 8000 pounds of food and thousands of dollars through the virtual food drive. Alameda County has one of the highest incidences of hunger in the nation. One of every five residents of the County call upon the Alameda Food Bank for assistance, and two-thirds of those requiring assistance are children and the elderly. Suggested food to be donated includes canned fruits, vegetables and meats; canned soup; peanut butter; pasta and canned pasta sauce. Even easier, participate in the Virtual Food drive by going to https:// tinyurl.com/2021VirtualFoodDrive and turn $1 into $6 to help the Scouts reach their goal of $5,000! For more information, contact Ellen Maloney Ruhe at the Scout office at 510-844-4752.

articles.text: Non-traditional vice mayorship selection in 2020 prompts discussion Piedmont’s City Council may change from its traditional selection process for mayor and vice mayor following an unorthodox selection one year ago in November 2020. Councilmembers discussed options at a November 1 meeting. The only written policy regarding how the mayor and vice mayor are selected is found in the section 2.08 of the City Charter, which states, “following each general municipal election, the City Council shall elect from among its member officers of the City who shall have the titles of Mayor and Vice-Mayor, each of whom shall serve at the pleasure of the Council.” For 30 years the city council has appointed the council member who has been re-elected for a second term as vice mayor and then mayor for two-year terms respectively. Additionally, seniority with city council would be the first qualifier of vice mayorship, and top votes received in an election as the second qualifier. This process has resulted in a twice-elected council member not having the opportunity to serve as vice mayor or mayor. Last year the role of Vice Mayor was dually assumed for the first time, with Tim Rood and Jen Cavenaugh designated as Vice Mayors in 2021-2022 and 2022- 2023 respectively. The City Council meeting on December 7, 2020 took an unorthodox turn when the council voted to split the position of vice mayor instead of it being a traditional two-year term. The city council voted to have Rood, a six-year member of the council, assume the title for one year followed by Cavenaugh for one year. Cavenaugh was the top vote-getter in 2016 and 2020, and Rood has seniority with six years on council. While it was ultimately decided by councilmembers that the vice mayorship would be “shared,” the decision was reached only after a lengthy discussion. The hiccup prompted groups like the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) and the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee (PADC) to author a letter to city council on December 11, 2020, pointing out a “lack of transparency and clarity” in the process. The groups called on city council to clearly write out rules and procedures and make them accessible to the public rather than “rely on institutional memory, or interpretation, to be passed along.” Moving forward At the November 1 meeting, Councilmember Conna McCarthy said that the traditional approach of “who gets the most votes is rather shallow.” In 2020, McCarthy, in response to the tradition of top vote-getting, said that a “vote for council is not a vote for mayor.” “I don’t see a groundswell of community dissatisfaction with the two-year rotation,” Councilmember Betsy Andersen offered. “But with respect to the key point of transparency, I would be an advocate of putting, in writing, what our customary practices have been for the past 30 years.” Andersen acknowledged that she was in favor last year of sticking to the traditional process, but added that it “leaves someone out. [It] doesn’t work with four-year terms and a five-year rotation.” Vice Mayor Tim Rood expressed gratitude to his colleagues for selecting him for the position following lengthy discussion in 2020. “I appreciate you having broken with tradition in allowing me to have this opportunity,” he said. To continue with a split-term option in these instances was floated among council, which Rood and Andersen favored. All councilmembers agreed that a written policy should be in place moving forward. Cavenaugh agreed that her preference would be to provide greater clarity. “Even though [this issue] only has come up a few times in the past 30 years, when it happens, it is meaningful. If there’s an opportunity to take our current system and improve upon it, whether that is sharing [the position] or greater clarity, I would be open to that,” she said. City Council directed City Administrator Sara Lillevand to compile a report by July 2022 that details options on how the city can establish a formal policy in writing.
articles.title: City may change traditional selection of Mayor, Vice Mayor

articles.text: The Piedmont City Council unanimously approved on November 1 a 3% salary increase for employees of the Public Works Department. The prior Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) expired in June 2021. The agreement for a pay raise will be in effect through June 30, 2025. Current and retired department employees also received modest increases to healthcare benefits. An update to bereavement leave now allows leave for purposes other than to attend funeral or memorial services. The total fiscal impact over the four-year period is $625,000. pages.text: Wednesday, November 10, 2021 3 City may change traditional selection of Mayor, Vice Mayor Non-traditional vice mayorship selection in 2020 prompts discussion By Allyson Aleksey Piedmont’s City Council may change from its traditional selection process for mayor and vice mayor following an unorthodox selection one year ago in November 2020. Councilmembers discussed options at a November 1 meeting. The only written policy regarding how the mayor and vice mayor are selected is found in the section 2.08 of the City Charter, which states, “following each general municipal election, the City Council shall elect from among its member officers of the City who shall have the titles of Mayor and Vice-Mayor, each of whom shall serve at the pleasure of the Council.” For 30 years the city council has appointed the council member who has been re-elected for a second term as vice mayor and then mayor for two-year terms respectively. Additionally, seniority with city council would be the first qualifier of vice mayorship, and top votes received in an election as the second qualifier. This process has resulted in a twice-elected council member not having the opportunity to serve as vice mayor or mayor. Last year the role of Vice Mayor was dually assumed for the first time, with Tim Rood and Jen Cavenaugh designated as Vice Mayors in 2021-2022 and 2022- 2023 respectively. The City Council meeting on December 7, 2020 took an unorthodox turn when the council voted to split the position of vice mayor instead of it being a traditional two-year term. The city council voted to have Rood, a six-year member of the council, assume the title for one year followed by Cavenaugh for one year. Cavenaugh was the top vote-getter in 2016 and 2020, and Rood has seniority with six years on council. While it was ultimately decided by councilmembers that the vice mayorship would be “shared,” the decision was reached only after a lengthy discussion. The hiccup prompted groups like the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) and the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee (PADC) to author a letter to city council on December 11, 2020, pointing out a “lack of transparency and clarity” in the process. The groups called on city council to clearly write out rules and procedures and make them accessible to the public rather than “rely on institutional memory, or interpretation, to be passed along.” Moving forward At the November 1 meeting, Councilmember Conna McCarthy said that the traditional approach of “who gets the most votes is rather shallow.” In 2020, McCarthy, in response to the tradition of top vote-getting, said that a “vote for council is not a vote for mayor.” “I don’t see a groundswell of community dissatisfaction with the two-year rotation,” Councilmember Betsy Andersen offered. “But with respect to the key point of transparency, I would be an advocate of putting, in writing, what our customary practices have been for the past 30 years.” Andersen acknowledged that she was in favor last year of sticking to the traditional process, but added that it “leaves someone out. [It] doesn’t work with four-year terms and a five-year rotation.” Vice Mayor Tim Rood expressed gratitude to his colleagues for selecting him for the position following lengthy discussion in 2020. “I appreciate you having broken with tradition in allowing me to have this opportunity,” he said. To continue with a split-term option in these instances was floated among council, which Rood and Andersen favored. All councilmembers agreed that a written policy should be in place moving forward. Cavenaugh agreed that her preference would be to provide greater clarity. “Even though [this issue] only has come up a few times in the past 30 years, when it happens, it is meaningful. If there’s an opportunity to take our current system and improve upon it, whether that is sharing [the position] or greater clarity, I would be open to that,” she said. City Council directed City Administrator Sara Lillevand to compile a report by July 2022 that details options on how the city can establish a formal policy in writing. The City’s Sustainability Division wants your feedback on EVs and EV Charging in Piedmont. All Piedmont residents are invited to share their input through an online EV community survey. It is anticipated that the survey will take 10-20 minutes to complete. All questions are optional, and responses will remain anonymous. The survey will be available until Friday, November 26. Responses will shape the EV priorities and actions residents will take in the coming years to address climate change and build a more resilient community. The City of Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan 2.0 provides a roadmap for reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in the community. A major goal of the plan is to eliminate emissions from the transportation sector, which has consistently comprised nearly half of Piedmont’s total GHG emissions. One strategy to achieve this is by accelerating the adoption of EVs and the growth of EV Charging Stations in Piedmont. The City has an ambitious target of 50% EV ownership by 2030 and 100% EV ownership by 2050. Currently, EVs account for 11% of the vehicles registered in Piedmont. On October 18, the City Council approved an agreement for the installation of four DC fast EV charging stations on Magnolia Avenue near the Exedra. Fill out the survey and help the Sustainability team identify where to prioritize the installation of the next group of EV chargers. The survey can be found online at https://docs.google.com/ forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSf1k7DeC9v L38AaVqAWlyPc011c9nlvs5Tj3orxS65jc-WPlw/viewform. articles.text: Editor: I read the clarification on the premium bond provisions in the city’s borrowing authority printed in the Piedmont Post on October 27. It notes that the city’s outside counsel assured staffers that the city has the authority to issue bonds at a premium dollar price, supported by an interest rate of up to 12%. Providing that response to the question posed in a letter previously printed in this paper is either naive or insincere, and in either case it is insulting. The premium proceeds amount to borrowing extra money which is repaid by committing the city to an above-market coupon, at least through the call date. The market yield for a Piedmont general obligation would be in the 3% area in today’s market; the 12% cap in the borrowing authority is standard boilerplate language designed to capture a range of market conditions over the long term, not to be a back door to borrowing as much as double the voter approved amount. The original letter to the Post was addressing the issue of the city borrowing even more than was originally and recently deemed necessary. When city employees quote lawyers to pretend to address a legitimate taxpayer question, while avoiding the substance of the question, we should all remind ourselves that tax paying Piedmont homeowners (not lawyers of staffers) are on the hook to pay this back.

articles.text: Bright and early Thanksgiving morning a hardy band of symphony musicians will arrive in Piedmont, set up their chairs and music stands in front of the Exedra, and announce –- musically – the start of the 20th annual Piedmont Turkey Trot, a traditional 5-kilometer run on city streets. It’s not a benefit – it’s a fun run embraced strongly by residents and people from throughout the U.S. who come to visit relatives. The big treat for runners (and spectators) this year will be the sign of eight symphony musicians from the Bay Area on hand to play music written for hunting horns 200 years ago. “We will have eight hunting horn players who will be playing on authentic trompes de chasse from France,” explained Piedmont resident Tom Reicher, a retired French Horn player with Berkeley Symphony. “Originally, the trompe de chasse was used as a loud signaling instrument that would communicate to hunters various aspects of the hunt. However, over more than two centuries music was developed for large ensembles of trompes de chasse, and that is what we will be playing. This is music intended to be performed outdoors and thus is appropriate to celebrate the gathering of runners for the Piedmont Turkey Trot.” Onlookers will see one with a very large circumference, called the trompe de chasse “Dauphine.” The trompe de chasse d’Orleans has a smaller circumference. The trompe de chasse Lorraine resembles an animal horn. But because they all are pitched in the key of D, they all have the same length of tubing – approximately 14 feet. Performing this year will be Robert Ward, principal horn, San Francisco Symphony; Piedmpnt resident Jonathan Ring, second horn, San Francisco Symphony; Daniel Hawkins, utility horn, San Francisco Symphony; Meredith Brown, principal horn, Oakland Symphony, Santa Rosa Symphony, Symphony Silicon Valley, and California Symphony; Caitlyn Smith, principal horn, Santa Cruz Symphony, Stockton Symphony, and Santa Rosa Symphony; Alicia Mastromonaco, section horn, Marin Symphony, Monterey Symphony, and Carmel Bach Festival; Piedmont resident Stuart Gronningen, retired principal horn, Oakland Symphony and Berkeley Symphony; and Reicher, the mastermind. As the word spread among horn players, the group has grown to an ensemble of eight.

articles.text: The American Red Cross is encouraging blood donors of all blood types - especially type O - to make an appointment now. To encourage donations this month, people giving blood through November 23 will receive a $10 Amazon Gift Card by email. As the holidays approach and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warns about a potential spike in flu cases this year, it’s important that those who are eligible, healthy and feeling well make an appointment to donate blood or platelets. The American Red Cross continues to address an ongoing emergency blood shortage, and donors are urged to give now to combat the lowest blood supply levels at this time of year in more than a decade. According to the CDC, flu cases reached an all-time low last year due to masking, physical distancing and shutdowns across the country, and many Americans may have reduced immunity this year. When seasonal illness increases, the number of healthy blood donors tends to decrease. Paired with winter weather, busy holiday schedules and ongoing COVID-19 concerns, the already-struggling blood supply could be further impacted throughout winter. There is no blood donation waiting period for those who have received a flu shot or a Moderna, Pfizer or Johnson & Johnson COVID-19 vaccine or booster, so long as donors are symptom-free. Donors are urged to schedule an appointment now by using the Red Cross Blood Donor App, visiting RedCrossBlood.org or calling 1-800-733-2767. The nearest Red Cross blood bank is at 6230 Claremont Avenue in Oakland. Tel. (800) 733-2767.

articles.text: During an October 27 Piedmont School Board meeting, Supt. Randy Booker declared he was lifting the outdoor mask requirement for students, staff, visitors, volunteers, consultants and contractors who provide proof of full vaccination against Covid-19. The change went into effect November 1. The change was not an action item so no vote was needed. However, Booker reminded the board that they could advise him to delay his declaration. The board was split on the issue. “I was 100% on board with removing the mask mandate until I talked with the nurses [and Dr. Rutherford],” board member Megan Pillsbury said. Board member Veronica Thigpen also questioned the removal of masks for the vaccinated when outdoors and brought up the difficulty of determining who is unvaccinated on campus. Booker A healthy number of PHS students on Tuesday still wore masks outdoors after school on campus, but most students were happy to have photos taken without a mask. 11th graders Violet Lemley and Brianna Sotelo show their pearly whites on the PHS campus after school on Tuesday, November 9. stated that there are very few kids who are unvaccinated, so the district can identify them. Board Member Hilary Cooper led the charge for supporting the removal of masks. She suggested that the mask requirement should be lifted for elementary age students too, regardless of vaccination status. “I’m wondering [how] we tell a first grader, you don’t have to wear a mask at the park, but you have to wear one playing [during] recess,” she said. After a passionate discussion, School Board President Cory Smegal took the reins and made convincing points to stick with Booker’s decision. “We are asking our vaccinated kids to run the mile with a mask on. I think the way Randy has set up this policy where we relax the mandate for our vaccinated students is right on target,“ she said. articles.text: I recently had the privilege of interviewing Barney Saltzberg for my Creative Parenting Podcast. He is the author of Beautiful Oops, which Bay Area Children’s Theatre adapted into a musical a few years ago. At one point in the interview, he casually said, “If you can’t draw a straight line, just draw a squiggly one.” And this has really stuck with me as such a critical viewpoint for parents as we raise our kids. I’m thinking of the straight line as the typical path – the one that is often thought of as “right”, and the squiggly one as the creative path, the non-traditional creative approach. How often do we try our hardest to “draw the straight line” as parents?! For instance, I am not great at tracking “the stuff” of kid rearing... the jackets, the permission slips. And I spend a lot of my time forcing myself to try to do it RIGHT! But what if I should be “drawing the squiggly line” and coming up with creative alternatives so that I don’t have to do something I’m just not that good at? Example: lining our front entryway with bins for kids to drop stuff in and then creating a nighttime ritual around “stuff sorting” while playing one of our favorite songs. Or making “stuff tracking” into a game, where my kids get a stone in a jar every What should success look like? time they find something without asking me for help? Fill the jar, get ice cream sundaes for dinner! Once we parents embrace that squiggly line, how can we apply the same practice to our kids? Allow them to accept that there are some things they do really well and other things that might require more creativity. The more we can give our kids the same freedom we give ourselves to not be perfect at everything, the easier it will be for them to love their strengths and their challenge zones. I think about my son who found the assignments in his art class very challenging but was thrilled when his teacher gave him permission to doodle whenever he needed to. The teacher liked the doodles so much that she accepted them as his art assignment. That’s truly the squiggly line in action. Nina Meehan is CEO of Bay Area Children’s Theatre. articles.text: Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir performs at Oakland Museum After a nearly two-year hiatus, the Piedmont East Bay Children Choir, a beloved local institution, finally returned to performing live on Saturday, October 30. It was a monumental event, given that the last two years of choir concerts were singers’ recorded voices mixed together and uploaded to YouTube. We can all agree nothing is the same when you’re sitting in a zoom meeting for over an hour. Looking back at the virtual choir season, every Tuesday and Thursday we would get on the Zoom call, camera off, zone out for two hours and log off. It was extremely hard to focus when nothing was happening besides someone talking through a computer. I still don’t understand how I remembered all the songs just by looking at the music and hearing the piano. This fall, when virtual rehearsals ended, it felt strange – but wonderful – to be within reach of each other. We had to get used to our voices again because on Zoom we never heard what we sounded like together. Because of the ever-looming threat of COVID-19, we have to wear special masks while singing that make us all look like ducks. I’m about four feet away from all of the people in my choir, so half the time I don’t know what people 15 feet away from me sound like. And the sound we make comes out muffled because of the masks, which means that we have to run through specific sections multiple times when rehearsing. Each time we sing the section, it sounds different. But I’ll take that any day over sitting in front of the computer screen. We’ve had enough of that. After rehearsing in person for two months the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir was ready for their first in-person concert in two years on October 30. It was the PEBCC Benefactor Gala to help raise money for the choi, the biggest event of the year, and was held at the newly created outdoor gardens at the Oakland Museum of California. Leading up to the concert, the senior levels of the choir had worked extremely hard to make sure the songs would be immaculate. Then there was the logistical part, where every part of the seating, food, and auction had to be tailored to perfection. Everybody at the PEBCC had an important job. The Gala started at 6 p.m., but the singers had to be there at 4 p.m., meaning a five-hour affair for the performers. It made me realize how much I missed being part of a live concert, when everybody is exhilarated and anxious, having fun with friends and waiting for their time on stage. After arriving, we went to the green room (dressing and rehearsal area) in the museum’s theater. It was modern, very airy and filled with light. The acoustics were perfect. We warmed up with singing drills, then ran through our songs until it was time for us to go on stage for a sound check. We returned to the green room for dinner. Pizza has never tasted so good. In addition to performing, members of the Ensemble got to wait on the tables and socialize with the benefactors. We worked in teams of five, forming a circle around tables and waiting for a guest to raise the slip of paper with the menu choice from the buffet. Being a waitress was hectic getting everyone’s orders in and bringing them back quickly. After we finished, all Ensemble kids headed to their tables in the back of the pavilion and sat down to watch Ancora perform their three songs. In the middle of the singing a fat rat ran right under our legs. Since there was a live performance, we couldn’t yell or scream, so we all had to stifle our shouts and not laugh too loudly about it. I have never seen a rat run as fast as that one did. Turned out it had a friend that watched us from above the garden stairs before a brave volunteer mother scared it away with a newspaper. When Ancora finished its performance to a long round of applause, the auction began. I did hear some prices that were way beyond my budget. After a final warm-up, we walked onstage. The lights were bright, the wind was cold, the exhaustion was there, and yet everyone was ready to sing. We sang three pieces, Hymn to Freedom, a piece with the message that no one is free until everyone is; Agnus Dei, a plea for mercy; and Bolo Bolo Sab Milo Bolo, a song about the god Shiva, written by Eric Tuan the choir’s Artistic Director I had never been more exhilarated. No matter how much I may have complained to my friends and family over the past year and a half, I had missed being a part of a choir. I could hear our sound during the performance: so strong, so full of emotion. For the first time in two years I felt like I was part of something bigger than one person, a choir and a community. I can’t wait to have more concerts, tours, and summer camps. Make no mistake, the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir is back. Larissa Edel, a freshman at Bentley School, has been a member of Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir for nine years.
articles.title: The return of live singing – with an audience

California’s public schools also rank among the lowest in the entire country in terms of teacher/pupil ratio, reading and math scores, and college readiness. But because Piedmont is so deeply committed to supporting our children and schools, the district has managed to buck those state trends. Support from the community has helped build a school system that consistently delivers small class sizes, high reading and math scores, and strong college preparedness. Over the past 30 years, the Piedmont community, including the 60% of Piedmont residents who don’t have children in schools, have repeatedly voted to approve local school parcel taxes, funding essential services to maintain excellence in our schools and keep Piedmont property values high. A question that often comes up is: “Why aren’t our schools fully funded by this parcel tax?” Piedmont’s school parcel tax supplies 25% of the funds for the schools, but that’s not enough to completely close the gap, especially given ever-rising costs. The additional support that the PUSD receives from the Giving Campaign is essential to maintain the schools’ educational excellence. Without the Giving Campaign and other fundraisers Piedmont’s schools would struggle to continue providing small class sizes, elective and AP classes, music and art programs, librarians, counselors, class aides, and other specialists. Those student resources help give children the stellar educational experience that they deserve. To learn more about the Giving Campaign and to make a donation, visit PiedmontEdFoundation.org/donate. It was a monumental event, given that the last two years of choir concerts were singers’ recorded voices mixed together and uploaded to YouTube. We can all agree nothing is the same when you’re sitting in a zoom meeting for over an hour. Looking back at the virtual choir season, every Tuesday and Thursday we would get on the Zoom call, camera off, zone out for two hours and log off. It was extremely hard to focus when nothing was happening besides someone talking through a computer. I still don’t understand how I remembered all the songs just by looking at the music and hearing the piano. This fall, when virtual rehearsals ended, it felt strange – but wonderful – to be within reach of each other. We had to get used to our voices again because on Zoom we never heard what we sounded like together. Because of the ever-looming threat of COVID-19, we have to wear special masks while singing that make us all look like ducks. I’m about four feet away from all of the people in my choir, so half the time I don’t know what people 15 feet away from me sound like. And the sound we make comes out muffled because of the masks, which means that we have to run through specific sections multiple times when rehearsing. Each time we sing the section, it sounds different. But I’ll take that any day over sitting in front of the computer screen. We’ve had enough of that. After rehearsing in person for two months the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir was ready for their first in-person concert in two years on October 30. It was the PEBCC Benefactor Gala to help raise money for the choi, the biggest event of the year, and was held at the newly created outdoor gardens at the Oakland Museum of California. Leading up to the concert, the senior levels of the choir had worked extremely hard to make sure the songs would be immaculate. Then there was the logistical part, where every part of the seating, food, and auction had to be tailored to perfection. Everybody at the PEBCC had an important job. The Gala started at 6 p.m., but the singers had to be there at 4 p.m., meaning a five-hour affair for the performers. It made me realize how much I missed being part of a live concert, when everybody is exhilarated and anxious, having fun with friends and waiting for their time on stage. After arriving, we went to the green room (dressing and rehearsal area) in the museum’s theater. It was modern, very airy and filled with light. The acoustics were perfect. We warmed up with singing drills, then ran through our songs until it was time for us to go on stage for a sound check. We returned to the green room for dinner. Pizza has never tasted so good. In addition to performing, members of the Ensemble got to wait on the tables and socialize with the benefactors. We worked in teams of five, forming a circle around tables and waiting for a guest to raise the slip of paper with the menu choice from the buffet. Being a waitress was hectic getting everyone’s orders in and bringing them back quickly. After we finished, all Ensemble kids headed to their tables in the back of the pavilion and sat down to watch Ancora perform their three songs. In the middle of the singing a fat rat ran right under our legs. Since there was a live performance, we couldn’t yell or scream, so we all had to stifle our shouts and not laugh too loudly about it. I have never seen a rat run as fast as that one did. Turned out it had a friend that watched us from above the garden stairs before a brave volunteer mother scared it away with a newspaper. When Ancora finished its Advertise Here! performance to a long round of applause, the auction began. I did hear some prices that were With the... Piedmont Post way beyond my budget. After a final warm-up, we walked onstage. The lights were bright, the wind was cold, the exhaustion was there, and yet everyone For more information on placing an ad call... 626-2468 or email: nancy@cmc-ads.com was ready to sing. We sang three pieces, Hymn to Freedom, a piece with the message that no one is free until everyone is; Agnus Dei, a plea for mercy; and Bolo Bolo Sab Milo Bolo, a song about the god Shiva, written by Eric Tuan the choir’s Artistic Director I had never been more exhilarated. No matter how much I may have complained to my friends and family over the past year and a half, I had missed being a part of a choir. I could hear our sound during the performance: so strong, so full of emotion. For the first time in two years I felt like I was part of something bigger than one person, a choir and a community. I can’t wait to have more concerts, tours, and summer camps. Make no mistake, the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir is back. articles.text: Over Halloween weekend local FIRST Robotics team 8033, Highlander Robotics, competed with their robot Whirlpool in their first in-person tournament since their inception in 2019. Chezy Champs is an annual three-day invitational hosted by Bellarmine College Prep in San Jose and has historically featured world class teams. This year was no different. Of the 39 teams invited, 26 were former World Champions. Teams traveled from as far away as Israel to compete against friends and rivals in what some saw as a stand in for the cancelled world championships in 2020 and 2021. In the crowded field, the rookie Highlanders turned heads. “I have been going to robotics competitions for six years. This was a whole new level and by far the best event I have ever attended! Top teams wanted to meet the bold new team from Piedmont running swerve drive and to see their unique climber,” said team manager, Helen Potter. The robot’s climbing mechanism was designed and built by Alex Ware, Alyssa Angsupanich, and Basia Young working with Mechanical mentor Klaus Zietlow. It features a wheel-driven cable track with carbon fiber hook and a ratcheting winch with paracord and was responsible for several of the team’s wins later in the tournament. Their team placed 15th of 39 after 10 qualifying rounds with a 7-3 record and advanced to the playoffs. In the playoffs they were eliminated by the top-seeded alliance from Israel, the eventual winner of the tournament. The Highlanders were recognized in the awards ceremony as the Most Improved Team. New recruits, Matteo Scano and Vaughn Khouri, performed well as the driver and mechanism operators. Alex Ware and Reece Beck along with mentor Frank Zhao expertly repaired and serviced their robot Whirlpool in the pits between matches. New software team members, Lewy Reece Beck, Alex Ware, Arun Brahma, Peter Stokes, Avery Chan in the Highlander pit. Whirlpool, the Highlander Robotics robot. Highlander team members in the stands. Seiden and Charlie Clowes, working with software mentor Kevin Clark, were able to solve software issues on the climber mechanism early in the qualification rounds which was critical for the Highlanders strong match performance. Jasper Tripp, scouting lead, led a team of students that gathered data on the opponents and alliance partners which provided critical information for each match. Team captain Charlie Lambert kept the team focused and worked closely with alliance partners to optimize performance and point contribution in each match. In the FIRST Robotics CompeWhirlpool (8033) outgains two other robots in the Chezy Champs competition.

During their first season in 2020, a founding team of 11 established basic skills and built a robot, named Nessie, to compete in the game Infinite Recharge which is centered around picking up and shooting dodge balls into targets before reaching an endgame where 125- pound robots grab a pull-up bar and lift themselves off the ground. The season was cancelled in response to COVID one week before their first competition. In 2021, the FRC format was adapted for an at-home virtual challenge and robots from the previous year were allowed. The Highlanders, now with 18 students for the new season, chose to build a more ambitious new robot, Whirlpool. It features a swerve drivetrain, the ability to shoot targets high in the air, and a mechanism that allowed the robot to hook a bar and lift itself off the ground. The team designed and built it in small groups in the Lambert garage and tested their software in Piedmont Middle School’s Morrison gym. In the Infinite Recharge At-Home competition, Whirlpool scored well in skills challenges and earned the team the Rookie Game Changer Award. By the fall this year, the Highlanders had grown to 27 students with a new leadership team after six seniors graduated last Spring. With hopes of being invited to Chezy Champs in the Fall, the team spent September and October training new recruits and preparing Whirlpool to compete. The new season begins on January 8, 2022 and the Highlanders will design and build a new robot to compete in the new challenge at UC Davis and San Jose State in March and April 2022. articles.text: Piedmont faces No. 2 Marin Academy today in Larkspur The No. 3 ranked Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team got the Division 2 North Coast Section playoffs started with a 7-3 win over No. 6 Terra Linda in the quarterfinals on Saturday, November 13 at Carondelet in Concord after receiving a firstround bye. “We’ve figured out that the best way for us to win games is to play really solid defense and not give up any counter-attack goals,” said coach John Savage. It was another strong defensive outing for the Highlanders forcing long shots towards PHS goalie Dariush Kashani. “That was the plan, to double team and help set and force shots from the perimeter. We wanted to force shots from their less experienced guys,” said Savage. The match featured Declan Linnane leading the offense with a 3-goal hat trick. The team’s seven goals came from three players, Linnane (3), Antonio Rivera (3) and Shane Miller. “Declan played really well. He’s starting to pick his spots effectively and realize that he has the speed to counter-attack. Offensively, he’s a facilitator and a driver. Because the other team is focused on our primary scoring options, Declan will have opportunities if he puts himself in the right position. He definitely did that on Saturday,” said Savage. 7-3 win over No. 6 Terra Linda Terra Linda opened the game with a goal at the end of the first quarter, but Piedmont powered back in the second quarter to jump ahead 3-2 before halftime. The Highlanders tacked on two unanswered goals in the third for a 5-2 advantage, and added two goals in the fourth for the 7-3 final. In the second quarter, nearly three minutes ran off the clock by the time Piedmont drew an exclusion and sent in a goal 25 seconds later from Antonio Rivera to tie it 1-1. Terra Linda’s Ben Shafer scored on their next possession. But Linnane scored the first of three goals with 2:58 remaining to tie it at 2-2. With 1:55 left in the half, Piedmont drew another exclusion to gain a 6-on-5 opportunity, Shane Miller scored after 13 seconds for a 3-2 lead at the half. Defense also reigned supreme in the third quarter with nearly half the quarter running off before Linnane scored with 3:39 remaining, 4-2. Rivera sent in Piedmont’s next goal with 2:21 left, 5-2. Piedmont successfully killed a penalty when Terra Linda drew an exclusion on Miller with 1:43 left. In the fourth, TL’s Daniel Buckley scored 36 seconds in, 5-3. But their joy was shortlived when Piedmont’s Linnane scored 16 seconds later, 6-3. Miller scored the final goal with a man-advantage with 3:46 left for the 7-3 final. articles.text: It was a rough way to end the season-finale at Mt. Eden in Hayward on Friday, November 5, as the Highlander were shutout 35-0 by the Monarchs. The team ended its season with 2-7 overall record and 2-4 in league. PHS trailed 7-0 at the end of the first period, 14-0 at halftime, and 28-0 at the end of the third quarter. Despite the Highlanders’ struggles this season, Piedmont fought valiantly with a depleted roster that fluctuated between 15-19 available players throughout the season. “The kids did not quit. They hung in mentally with those small roster numbers. At any given time they could have walked away, but they didn’t. That’s a testament of the kids. Generally when numbers are low, morale goes down. But they understood what we were in for and pushed forward,” said coach Jerome Johnson. Johnson had high praise of seniors Ethan Feldstein, Mason Kimball, and Nico Defazio for their toughness this fall. “Ethan and Mason were threeyear varsity players and understood what it took. They led by example, Ethan played fearlessly through a shoulder and finger injury, and all types of aches and bruises. He showed what it took to maintain a level of excellence through the pain. Nico Defazio he hung in there through pain, had finger surgery, and wanted to come back immediately. He fought through it and came back for the finale,” said Johnson. Despite the loss, a bright spot was the school’s quarterback of the future, freshman Markos Lagios, getting the start. He rushed for nearly 90 yards and also passed for nearly 100 yards. “What I love about him is that he’s very mature for only being 15. He’s never played tackle football and we knew things were going to move faster for him. We wanted to get him the experience of seeing the speed of varsity football,” said Johnson. Lagios is characterized by his speed and strong arm – a common trait of the modern quarterback. Although he faces critiques of being “undersized,” Johnson is confident that Lagios has loads of potential. “To lead an offense, you have to lead by example and out-work everybody else. I know he’s ready for it. We’re looking for him to learn how to read defenses this offseason and we’ll get that time in. I’ve told him so many quarterbacks have been undersized and it doesn’t matter; he has the tools to get it done,” said Johnson. Looking ahead, the Highlanders will return some vital players to the lineup, including brothers Bautista and Matteo Costa, who at running back and linebacker will be back as seniors. Defensive lineman Bailey Cain and receiver/ defensive back Ryan McConathy will also be senior leaders. “The Costa brothers will be a major focal-point, same with Bailey Cain and Ryan McConathy. Those are going to be the guys we focus on and will be major points of what we do next season. They will all be great leaders for the team,” said Johnson. Bautista Costa is seen as a key player on next year’s team. Photos by Mike McConathy Piedmont wraps up its season after falling to Mt. Eden last Friday. articles.text: The Piedmont tennis team traveled to Chabot College in Hayward for the Western Alameda County Conference Championship Tournament on Friday and Saturday, November 5-6. No. 1 singles player Bridgette McEfee reached the singles finals, and Amanda Becker and Audrey Mahany placed fourth in the doubles bracket. “We would have liked two second-place finishes, but it’s still a good result. Bridgette did really well to reach the finals,” said PHS coach Jim Landes. McEfee entered as the No. 3 seed and received a first-round bye. She defeated Alameda’s Nisha Johnson 6-1, 6-2 in the quarterfinals on Friday, then followed with a gritty 6-4, 7-6 (7-5) semifinal win on Saturday, upsetting No. 2 Maya Curry of Berkeley. Facing O’Dowd’s talented No. 1 ranked sophomore Polina Marakhtanova in the finals, McEfee lost 6-0, 6-2. “Against Maya Curry, we split Staff Photo Jim Landes (left), Corey Reich, Bridgette McEfee, and Neil Rothenberg gather for a photo after McEfee’s second-place finish in singles in the WACC Championship Tournament. the last two matches and they both went to three-sets. I went into this match thinking I had to absorb the ball because I wasn’t going to beat her off groundstrokes and winners. So I was going for consistency, playing my Photo by Brian Mahany Amanda Becker and Audrey Mahany placed fourth in the doubles ladder. best, and keeping up my energy,” said McEfee. McEfee’s consistency got the best of her Berkeley counterpart. It came through in the second set with a late comeback after trailing 5-4, gaining a game as the server before stealing another game as the returner. McEfee held match point at 6-5, but Curry tied as the returner 6-6 to force a seven-point tiebreaker. In the breaker, the two players traded games until reaching 5-5, when McEfee went ahead on another long rally, 6-5. With match point as the returner, McEfee sent a hard backhand to the feet of Curry after the Yellowjackets’ starter began to approach the net. Curry was unable to make solid contact on the ball, and it was over. “I just focused on keeping things consistent, trying out some new shots. I got a little tired in the second set; she started hitting really well and the tiebreak was stressful, but it was fun,” said McEfee after her big win. In the finals, McEfee squared off with Marahtanova for the third time this season, resulting in the No. 1 seed from Bishop O’Dowd claiming a 6-0. 6-2 win and championship banner. McEfee marks the second-straight Piedmont singles starter to reach the finals after Makenna Thiel won last spring’s championship. articles.text: Photo courtesy of Thoughtsicle.com Tyson Lake is the only surface body of water in Piedmont. It is estimated to have 3 million gallons of water, and was the site of drowning victims in 1951 and 1952. With Halloween having come and gone, here’s some spooky history that took place in Piedmont many years ago. Tyson Lake is a small reservoir located between private residences on La Salle and Sotelo Avenues, tucked quietly behind Hampton Field. The location is not public property but is the only body of water in Piedmont. It’s not a lake for fishing and is possibly better known for two drowning tragedies that took place in the 1950s. On July 20, 1951, the Oakland Tribune reported that the Alameda County coroner’s jury recommended that Tyson Lake, an unused reservoir, be drained or properly fenced to prevent further accidents following the drowning of 17-year-old James Richards four days earlier. But nearly one year to the day of the first accident, a second young man drowned. On July 10, 1952 19-year old Donald Stracner drowned while swimming with two companions. John Haubner, a former Piedmont Police Officer and a Navy diver in World War 2, was called on to retrieve Stacner’s body. “As search for the body continued, Police Chief William Pflaum said he will “definitely recommend that some action be taken to alleviate this menace to life,” the Tribune wrote. On August 8, 1952, the City of Piedmont urged the 20 homeowners surrounding the lake to erect a fence around the lake to prevent future drownings. articles.text: Oakland Symphony’s opening concert of the 2021-2022 season is on Friday, November 19, and features pianist Lara Downes performing Florence Price’s Piano Concerto. The program also includes William Grant Still’s In Memoriam: The Colored Soldiers Who Died for Democracy, and Beethoven’s Symphony No. 3 (Eroica). Downes is among the foremost American pianists of her generation, a trailblazer on and off-stage whose musical roadmap seeks inspiration from the legacies of history, family, and collective memory. Downes’ playing has been called “ravishing” by Fanfare Magazine, “luscious, moody and dreamy” by the New York Times, and “addicting” by the Huffington Post. As a chart-topping recording artist, a powerfully charismatic performer, a curator and tastemaker, Downes is recognized as a cultural visionary on the national arts scene. Her forays into the broad landscape of American music have created a series of acclaimed recordings, including America Again, selected by NPR as one of “10 Albums that Saved 2016,” and hailed as “a balm for a country riven by disunion” by the Boston Globe. Her recent Sony Classical debut release For Lenny debuted in the Billboard Top 20 and was awarded the 2017 Classical Recording Foundation Award. In 2020, Downes celebrated the Year of the Woman with world premieres of newly discovered works by Florence Price and Margaret Bonds, and large-scale commissions from Paola Prestini and Clarice Assad, in collaboration with the Chicago Symphony and the Louisville Orchestra. articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California will present an exhibition celebrating Edith Heath, designer and founder of Heath Ceramics, beginning this Saturday, November 13. Edith Heath: A Life in Clay showcases the legacy of the artist with over 50 pieces of her ceramics, clay samples, photographs, and personal memorabilia on display. A documentary video will be shown inside the museum as well. The new exhibition introduces visitors to the artist’s career, which was deeply expressive of California’s land and lifestyle. Heath, who died in 2005, focused on creating dependable and long-lasting products for the home, with a focus on sustainability. A Life in Clay is organized by Curator of Photography Drew Johnson, and guest curator Jennifer Volland. The exhibition will be on display through June 2022. “Edith Heath transformed our notion of ‘good design’ pioneering a new aesthetic of natural, stylish yet functional products made from local materials and designed to endure,” said Johnson. “As an icon of quintessential California design who lived and worked in Sausalito and San Francisco, OMCA is excited to share the extraordinary story of Heath’s life and legacy.” Edith Heath Photo courtesy of University of California, Berkeley A Life in Clay examines Heath’s technical experimentations with native California clays and glaze formulas. Her love of natural landscapes shaped the quality of her design and inspired her to seek clays from California rather than what was traditionally used for dinnerware. “What began as a rebellion against imported white clay more than 50 years ago is now a modern-day classic,” said Volland, who has researched the artist since 2014 and served as an essayist for the book Edith Heath: Philosophies. To purchase tickets and learn more about the exhibition, visit www.museumca.org.

articles.text: Aurora Theatre Company’s production of “Father/Daughter” will premiere live this Friday, November 12, and will be available to stream December 7-12. Written by playwright Kait Kerrigan and directed by M. Graham Smith, the play is a contemporary romance featuring two actors playing two pairs of lovers, detailing how parents and children can impact romantic lives. The play is a recipient of the Edgerton Foundation New Play Award, which allows productions extra time for development and rehearsal through a monetary grant. Kerrigan, an award-winning playwright and lyricist, is best-known for We Have to Hold Hands and Mad Ones. “Kait Kerrigan’s writing is insightful, audacious, and liable to make you either laugh or cry when you least expect it,” said Aurora Artistic Director Josh Costello. Playwright Kait Kerrigan Aurora Theatre will host a post-event discussion with the playwright on Friday, November 19, and Tuesday, November 23, and also on December 1 and 9. Associate Artistic Director Dawn Monique Williams will moderate the discussion, and may be joined by actors, directors, or other community members. articles.text: Berkeley Marina Artist Michael Stehr, a Piedmont native, will present a new exhibit, The Other Side of the Fence: Considering Green and the Power of Color, at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The exhibit is dedicated in loving memory of the artist’s mother. Bonnie Drewes Stehr, who recently died. Gallery hours are Saturdays and Sundays, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. from November 13 to 21. A reception will be held on Friday evening, November 12. To attend the reception, RSVP to Michael at mstehrart@gmail.com. Red is hot, blue is cold, and yellow was known to make Van Gogh smile. While our reaction to color is affected greatly by personal preference, there is no denying that color has the ability to make one feel while eliciting a tangible reaction. In this exhibit Stehr explores the power of color by focusing on the impact of green. In 1140, stained glass at Notre Dame de Chartres showing Christ on the cross has the crucifix depicted in a green color, despite the fact that we know the cross was made of wood and was likely a shade of brown. Of course, green is associated with life ... rolling green hills in Spring, a lush forest, or a perfectly manicured baseball field ... all images that can elicit feelings of growth, vitality, and renewal. The cross depicted as green refers to the renewal that one’s soul can experience due to the sacrifice of Jesus on that cross. We encounter green in our daily lives in various shades. There is the brilliant green of a lawn encountered in morning light. There is the neutralized green of an oak tree that can almost appear warm under the light of early evening. Furthermore, the greens one perceives in a foreground change greatly when viewing them at a distance. The exhibit will include 30 new paintings in which the color green has an important role in the impact of the painting. Stehr will address the chemistry of green as he discusses how he mixes green to achieve the various effects. Also being exhibited are 45 paintings from previous exhibitions.

articles.text: Thomas Hardy wrote Far From the Madding Crowd in 1874 during the height of the Victorian era. It was a time when women deferred to the wishes of men and were considered property to be acquired and then ignored. Men, in contrast, offered women safe harbor and financial security. Hardy’s story has proved to be resilient and some might say timeless if not prescient. It is in great part because Hardy created in the character of Bathsheba Everdene as an atypical woman who is resiliently independent, desiring to live on her own terms and not those dictated by a husband. She declares to a suitor that she wishes to be no man’s property. The film, starring Carey Mulligan as Bathsheba, is not only beautifully photographed, but Mulligan shines as she conveys the emotions of a woman who inherits a large farm and the title of mistress of all she surveys. She is determined to “astonish” all who now work for her and make a success of the farm. She is not a dilettante but a woman who wishes to live on her own terms in a society where women are cloistered by custom and social mores. For all of her sturdy values and willingness to work hard in the fields, she is also a woman of emotions and passions. Hardy brings this to the fore when Bathsheba finds herself desired by three men, each vastly different. One is the farm’s shepherd, Gabriel Oak (Matthias Schoenaerts), a quiet man who has no station in life but is ever willing to step into the breach when needed. The second is a wealthy gentleman farmer, William Boldwood (Michael Sheen), whose vast holdings run parallel to Bathsheba’s farm. Impulsively, she sent him a Valentine’s Day card and the result was more than she bargained for. The third is a soldier, Sgt. Francis Troy (Tom Sturridge), bedecked in scarlet and gleaming helmet. He is someone who stirs her emotions that prove to be reckless and far removed from her practical and grounded approach to all other aspects of life. Suddenly this 19th century woman begins to lose her moorings and is confronted with a series of choices that most women of that era could never have imagined. Her vulnerability stems from a confused heart, not from a lack of financial independence. She is, in effect, the female equivalent of William Boldwood, who also makes a life changing decision. How Bathsheba sorts out this existential moment makes for a genuinely fine narrative, delivered by an excellent cast. As a period film, Far From the Madding Crowd is compelling and solidly engaging. Tangentially, the Brits adapted Hardy’s novel in 1967. Directed by John Schlesinger, the film starred Julie Christie, Alan Bates, Peter Finch and Terence Stamp. At the time it was considered definitive (almost three hours), as well as a tour de force portrayal by Christie whose startling beauty gave the film a far different look than this recent incarnation. Mulligan is in many ways a more interesting casting choice, her independence and allure drawn from her convictions and not overshadowed by her appearance. Far From the Madding Crowd. Starring Carey Mulligan, Mathias Schoenaerts, Michael Sheen. 1 hr., 58 min. Rated PG-13.

He packs with studied efficiency, breezes through lines, swipes his cards, flashes his ID and is soon ensconced on the next flight, happily on his way to the next series of firings. He brags that he spends 322 days on the road and is miserable the other 43 days. He has no home to speak of – his apartment looks like an impersonal hotel room – and no connections to anyone, though he has a sister. He turns the idea of the lonely crowd on its head and his solitary life into an enthusiastic preference absent even a hint of angst. What is so superb about the film is that Bingham is an executioner and the audience is completely beguiled by his smile and intelligence and wit. He never pauses to unpack his emotions or reflect on the impact of his task and for a good part of the film neither does the audience. But then two women enter his life, one a businesswoman, Alex (Vera Farmiga), and Natalie (Melanie Lyskey), a new hire at his company. Alex he meets in a hotel lounge. Natalie is sent on the road with him to learn the ropes, so to speak. Both challenge his view of life, his contented detachment, and his elaborate rationales for his choices. Incrementally, the audience begins to sense that Bingham’s carefully manicured existence may not be as tightly compacted as first assumed. Though the film focuses all but exclusively on Bingham, so likable, so nicely constructed, and perhaps so starkly alone, the real tragedy resides with those he fires. Reitman includes snapshots of non-actors who have been recently let go, asking them to look into the camera and share what it means to loose their jobs after a decade or more. We watch as their faces crumble and they run the gauntlet of emotions and we can all but hear a door slamming shut. They are the subtext this film. For the most part disguised but also ever-present. Indeed, Surf’s Up is a fun, family-oriented, computer-animated tale about a teenage rockhopper penguin named Cody Maverick (Shia LaBeouf) who has always dreamed of being a world-class surfer ever since he met, some years ago, the legendary wave rider Big Z/Geek Topanga. Hence, he can often be found riding waves offshore near the town of Shiverpool, where he lives with his mother Edna (Dana Belben) and his brother Glen (Brian Posehn). One day a reality film crew arrives to make a documentary film about surfing. And so the feature becomes a faux documentary (perhaps a parody) in which the surfers talk in dude speak into the camera. Along with the film crew is Mikey Abramowitz (Mario Cantone), a talent scout, who is looking for possible entrants to compete in the Big Z Memorial surfing contest, to be held on the Hawaiian-style island of Pen-Gu. Cody jumps at the chance to enter and soon is off to the island. Along the way he befriends Chicken Joe (Jon Heder), a gnarly, good-natured caricature of a serious denizen of the surf world. Almost immediately upon arriving on the island, Cody meets a lovely lifeguard, Lani Allikai (Zooey Deschanel), a gentoo penguin, who rescues him from the surf and takes him to meet her uncle, Geek (Jeff Bridges), who helps Cody shape a new surfboard in preparation for the contest. He even helps train him, all while injecting some life lessons, reminding the teen that surfing is about having fun as well as winning. Cody’s main rival for the championship is Tank “The Shredder” Evans (Diederich Bader), a dude who has won the annual contest for almost a decade. Cody wants to win, especially to impress Lani. The event is run by a scheming rodent voiced by James Wood. Surf’s Up is a wonderful feature, steeped in surfing culture and lingo, with a lush backdrop, lots of imaginative characters, a gorgeous blue ocean, plus some great action scenes. Kids will be thoroughly entertained. Surf’s Up. Directed by Ash Brannon and Chris Buck. With Voices of Shia LaBeouf, Jeff Bridges, and Zooey Deschanel. Sony computer animation. 1 hr., 25 min. articles.text: Wall-E, an animated collaboration between Pixar animation studios and Disney, debuted in theaters in 2008. It was a huge hit then as it should be now with a new generation of youngsters. Kids will be enamored with this small, irresistible tin box named WALL-E (Ben Burtt), who has binoculars for eyes that are not only functional, but capable of a panoply of emotive expressions. We watch him scoot around the dusty, dystopian remains of an uninhabited, litter-strewn earth on tractor-like wheels. Apparently, he was left behind to collect and compact the detritus of the longago departed humans. The name WALL-E is actually an acronym for Waste Allocation Load Lifter-Earth Class, which captures his day-in and day-out job. The year is 2700, and the planet has long ago been abandoned by its residents, who now live on a massive cruise ship-like space station called Axiom, which is run by a big box corporation, Buy N’ Large, and managed by robots who service the denizens’ every need. The humans move about in large hover recliners, have grown fat and lazy, wanting only to consume and watch their individual screens while drinking milkshakes. Meanwhile, back on earth, it becomes clear that WALL-E feels deeply his isolation and loneliness, made evident by the way he peruses the memorabilia left behind. He has a place of his own where he keeps old light bulbs, hubcaps, a Zippo lighter, and one of his favorite items, a Rubik’s cube. He often spends time in his digs, accompanied only by a tenacious cockroach, watching old Gene Kelly videos. To his surprise, an unmanned probe is sent to earth from Axiom named EVE (Elissa Knight), an Extra-terrestrial Vegetation Evaluator. She is sleekly designed, looks like an iPod, and beeps. Her purpose is to determine if there is any hope of the humans returning to the rust-colored planet and reestablishing any kind of organic life. Of course, from the get-go, WALL-E is smitten with EVE, and gives her some seedlings and a small plant he has found in his travels. EVE, having discovered what she was looking for, lifts off for Axiom. Naturally, WALL-E follows her, and thus begins the manic second half of the story that asks the questions whether EVE and WALL-E will end up together, and will the lazy humans decide to return to earth (a violation of the A113 “never return directive”) and begin the process of transforming the urban desolation they created centuries before back into something that resembles the once blue planet. Kids will definitely tune-in to find out. WALL-E. Directed by Andrew Straton. Pixar animation studios. With voices of Ben Burtt, Elissa Knight, Jeff Garvin. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated G. articles.text: Part 32 in a biweekly series As we have discussed in previous columns, the scope of design in our built environment covers a huge range, encompassing everything from large city and regional planning all the way down to things like the entry hardware on doorways – and everything in between. In the last column we reviewed the concept of “massing” which can be considered the macro scale of building design. This week we move to the other end of the spectrum, architectural detailing which is building design at the micro scale. The combination of form and function, art and engineering that defines architecture is very evident in building detailing. Not only do the waterproofing details have to keep the water out, they also must fit into the aesthetic and must look nice. The famous modernist architect Ludwig Mies van der Rohe is often credited with first stating the familiar maxim: “God is in the details”, underscoring their importance in no uncertain terms. As a visually supportive component they can enhance and reinforce an overall design concept or, if not thought through, compromise or even undermine it. All buildings contain a multitude of systems that include structural, plumbing, electrical, and HVAC (heating, ventilating and air conditioning) to name just a few. These numerous different systems must be coordinated and designed to accommodate their spatial and functional needs. articles.text: Te-Ping Chen presented her collection of short stories Land of Big Numbers to the First Mondays Reading Group on November 1. The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group held a zoom meeting on November 1 to discuss Land of Big Numbers written by Te-Ping Chen. Through an invitation by group member Albert Chen, a cousin of the author, Chen was invited to speak with the group on November 1 and she accepted. This special discussion drew a strong showing of 16 regular readers, and first-time reader Betsy Lim. Te-Ping Chen was a correspondent in the Wall Street Journal’s Beijing bureau for four years from 2014 to 2018. All but two of the 10 stories in her book are set inside China. There are countless, potential stories within this land, but Chen’s Land of Big Numbers offers a window into ordinary life in China. The stories are based on her experiences and understanding of the Chinese people and society that come from her reporting and a fertile imagination. Story examples include a young woman from the countryside who finds work in a Shanghai flower shop and daydreams about the lives of her well-off customers; a farmer who seeks to build an airplane from metal scraps; a delicious fruit that is deemed dangerous by the authorities; and a chef who tries and fails to understand his twin sister’s political activism. Another story examines how people may trade away their free will in exchange for comforts provided by the state. Land of Big Numbers received very positive critical review. The members of the group liked it and had many questions for Chen. Before the author joined the zoom call, Albert Chen provided some background on his younger cousin, who grew up in Oakland, attended Head Royce and then Brown University. She received a Fulbright Scholarship to study Chinese in rural China, and then a job with the Wall Street Journal in Hong Kong. To Albert’s consternation, she was transferred from Hong Kong to Beijing, far more dangerous, and reported from there for four years. The group was impressed with her writing. Her stories and the voices in them were different and timeless. They provided insight in portraying an authoritarian society and culture. Her stories are a collection of realism, allegory, magical realism, and fables. The tone in some of the stories is dystopian using it to convey what everyday peoples’ lives are like in China today. Some readers found the stories of life in repressive China to be depressing. Others liked the short story format but wanted to know more about the characters and what happened to them. Chen leaves her readers wanting more, a device used by good writers of short stories. When Chen joined the zoom call with the reading group, she provided more information about herself. As a reporter she spent her days collecting stories about life in China and included the richness in the lives of people in her stories in the book. The Communist state provides a degree of wellbeing for people, so most of them find their life acceptable and satisfying. Their lives may be comfortable, but it does come at a “dark fairy tale” cost to their personal freedom. Chen said that state control is only a fraction of the experience in China, but it is quite real. The older generation may have more of a challenge with this new China because their early communist lives were more idealistic. Younger people are enjoying the country’s new, higher standard of living, and new, zany lifestyles. However, Chen left the First Mondays readers with a sense of hope in her last story, a story about people in China who value freedom and want to live free. Chen is now the Wall Street Journal’s reporter in Philadelphia. She lives there with her husband and their young child and is working on a novel. The readers were impressed that this delightful, young woman, whose verbal communication is as eloquent and fluid as in her written words, is able to manage her several worlds so fully and effectively. Everyone is looking forward to the publication of her new book and reading it. Before ending the November discussion, the group confirmed that its selection of December is Michael Lewis’ non-fiction, The Premonition: A Pandemic Story. The January selection will be Hamnet, a novel by Maggie O’Farrell. Alternating fiction and non-fiction, the group chose The Boys in the Boat by Daniel James Brown, a 2013 New York Times bestseller, for their February book. The next discussion will be Monday, December 6, and will start at 1:30 p.m. Weather permitting, the group will meet in person at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome to join the group. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required at jwilk@piedmont.ca.gov. Michael Lewis’ non-fiction, The Premonition: A Pandemic Story is the December selection.

articles.text: Eye to Eye founder discusses his student mentorship program David Flink, a new Piedmont resident and founder of Eye to Eye, has been named a 2021 CNN Hero for his work in launching and maintaining a unique mentorship program. The company has grown from a college service project in 1998 to what is now a national program used in 150 schools in 22 states across the country and impacting more than 1,350 students each week. The program pairs college-aged and high school-aged mentors with younger students who experience learning differences that may adversely impact their successes in school. At least 20% of the students have some kind of learning difference, which ranges from Attention Deficit Disorder (ADD) to Dyslexia and other processing deficits. “It is Eye to Eye’s belief and has always been our belief, that young people who learn differently are our leaders,” Flink said. “The power to lead this movement rests with them. In 1998, when Eye to Eye first began. I was one of those college students with a learning difference and I believed I had a story to share that could help.” – David Flink, Founder of Eye to Eye The program grew through word of mouth. When considering the mission behind the organization, Flink said he envisions Eye to Eye as a “world where young people can be seen and heard and valued.” Living with dyslexia – a learning disorder that involves difficulty reading and with specific language skills – has shaped his vision for the mentorship program. “Elementary school was an isolating and difficult experience, to say the least. I did not know other people who had learning disabilities,” he explained. “When I think about the vision of Eye to Eye … it was very much shaped around the idea that I looked for mentors [and] peers who also had learning differences.” The mentorship model targets middle school students following a multi-year study done with UC San Francisco, which shows that most students have trouble with self-identity and self-esteem in those years, especially those with learning differences. “The study looked at where Eye to Eye existed and found the program protected students from depression and enhanced their sense of community and self-worth. We focus on middle school because we know that that’s a ripe opportunity to help young people who both need the help urgently but also are receptive to the idea that they can take on greater power in owning their learning and being an advocate for themselves and making the David Flink best of the opportunities in front of them,” Flink explained. Rather than creating an academic tutor approach, the organization hones in on effectiveness of a mentor-mentee relationship. Mentors help their younger counterparts by being supportive through the learning process, and by offering real anecdotal leadership. “Eye to Eye’s secret sauce is that our mentors don’t need to be trained on what it means to have a learning difference,” Flink said. “This is really important. Our mentors always show up with a sense of authenticity and are always able to tell stories from their own lives that connect directly with their mentees’ experiences. Our job is to help them understand what it means to work with young people.” Each summer, the organization partners with universities and high schools that select two student leaders for their respective “chapters.” The chosen student leaders then take part in a one-week training program at Brown University that teaches them leadership skills through workshops and community building. Flink was unaware that, for years, mentors and supporters had nominated him and his organization to be recognized by CNN’s Heroes of the Year, which honors people who show extraordinary will to act on their values to improve the lives of others. All 10 nominated individuals in this year’s lineup receive $10,000 for their cause, and the individual who receives the most “votes” will receive an additional $100,000. Flink explained that more financial resources means that the organization will be able to reach more students, including allowing Eye to Eye to reach more historically Black colleges and Hispanic institutions from which it could attract mentors to work with mentees from similar backgrounds. “My intention is if we’re able to get this $100,000 and have that exposure on the national stage, [it would] show that people who learn differently are everywhere,” Flink said. “This is an opportunity to give a spotlight to young people who were invisible before the pandemic, who were further hidden behind screens and masks during the pandemic, and who still need a safe space so that they can feel seen, heard, and valued. The opportunity to support these young people every single day has been an absolute honor. I see them as the leaders who are keeping this organization moving forward.” You can vote for Flink’s organization, and learn more about the other nominated individuals, by visiting: www.cnn.com/specials/cnn-heroes.
